Expectation1: Diagnose patient illnesses accurately based on symptoms and tests
Situation1: A patient with symptoms of the common cold has come in for a routine check-up.
Expectation2: Raise public awareness about social inequities and marginalized groups
Situation2: They respond to an urgent incident of discrimination that requires immediate public attention and awareness.
Story: I sat across from Mrs. Lee, her voice raspy as she described her sore throat and runny nose. As her doctor, I listened carefully, noting her symptoms and reviewing her chart. My mind ticked through possible diagnoses, determined to ensure nothing serious was overlooked. I owed her my full attention, my expertise, my care. But as I reached for my stethoscope, my phone buzzed urgently. A message from the advocacy group flashed on the screen: a local shelter had just denied entry to several unhoused people, citing discriminatory policies. They needed me—my voice, my presence, my outrage—right now, to help shine a light on this injustice. I felt the weight of both worlds pressing in. Mrs. Lee’s expectant eyes met mine, trusting me to focus on her health. Yet, the faces of those turned away from shelter haunted me, demanding I act. My heart pounded as I wrestled with the impossible choice: to be the doctor my patient needed, or the advocate my community depended on.
